back: The sense of who a person is: name, family, totem, language, culture, community and nation.
A work party in which neighbours help one household with a big task; the host provides food and drink.
The chief's granary: a communal field whose grain fed orphans, widows, the elderly and the community in drought.
A ceremony held before the rains to ask God and the ancestors for rain.
An all-night ceremony with mbira music, singing and dancing to communicate with ancestral spirits.
A ceremony held some time after burial at which the spirit of the deceased is believed to be brought home.
Drums, mbira, rattles (hosho), clay pots (also ceremonial axes, staffs, cloths).

front: How does the family shape identity, compared with the community?
back: The family gives who you are (name, totem, history, language); the community gives where you belong (shared customs, events, norms).

front: Give three reasons indigenous gatherings matter.
back: They build identity and belonging; provide social security; pass on culture (also religious expression, conflict resolution).
